case.lens: The plant supplies drinking water to a coastal city. The upgrade also installed a vendor's AI alarm assistant. It is a learned anomaly detector. It labels each pressure alarm “likely sensor fault” or “likely real excursion” with a confidence score. Tonight it labels the alarms “likely sensor fault, 0.91”. Two operators have started treating that label as a second opinion. Keep asking: does the label count as evidence?

transfer.title: Transfer case · the textbook's two flight-control architectures
transfer.text: The textbook contrasts two certified aircraft. Airbus flight control uses redundant and diverse software. The Boeing 777 flight control has no software diversity. Both aircraft are certified as safe. This is a different system from the desalination plant.
transfer.source: Source slide 30 (problems with redundancy and diversity)
transfer.question: Without software diversity, what does the Boeing 777 design rely on for dependability?
transfer.answer: Simplicity and extensive verification and validation. The textbook notes that diversity adds complexity and new interactions. Both routes are accepted by regulators. Each needs its own evidence.
transfer.concept: simplicity versus diversity as dependability strategies

X01.answerKey: reliability and safety, not availability alone
X01.commonError: Students answer “availability” because the service responds. Ask which property covers a correct result, and which covers harm.

X02.answerKey: an observation that separates two hypotheses
X02.commonError: Students blame the software because an upgrade happened. Ask which log would separate a sensor fault from a software defect, and whether it exists.
X02.answer: Possible hypotheses include a faulty pressure transmitter, a defect in the upgrade, or a misleading alarm or hand-over procedure. Compare an independently verified pressure reading with the alarm and switch-over log. That could separate a true excursion from a sensor problem. These are hypotheses and requested observations, not completed tests.

X07.answerKey: fault activated, wrong state, visible deviation
X07.commonError: Students write “the system failed because of a software error”, which names two terms and explains neither. Correct the order: fault, error, failure.
X07.sourceLabel: Course addition · not from the textbook · applies the chapter to the case

X02A.commonError: Students merge tolerance and recovery. Tolerance keeps service going while faults occur; recovery restores service after a failure.

X03.answerKey: a correct controller inside an undependable service
X03.commonError: Traces stop at the application layer. Push upward: the shift hand-over is a business process and the regulator's file is society.
X03.question: Trace the alarm from equipment through software to people. Why can a correct controller still be part of an undependable service?

CHECK1.answerKey: reliability failed; safety depends on harm
CHECK1.commonError: Students answer “availability” for a reachable service with wrong results. Ask which property is about a correct result.
CHECK1.takeaway: A reachable service that returns the wrong result has failed in reliability, not availability.
CHECK1.question: A service is reachable but returns the wrong result. Which property failed?
CHECK1.sourceLabel: Course addition · not from the textbook · applies the chapter to the case

R08.commonError: Students treat two copies as independent by default. Make one student argue the no-diversity position; ask what the copies share.

lists.title: Redundancy and diversity
items: Redundancy: keep more than one version of critical components, so a backup is available if one fails
Diversity: provide the same function in different ways, so components do not fail in the same way
Independence: redundant and diverse components must not share common-mode failures, for example by using different programming languages

lists.title: Examples
items: Redundancy: where availability is critical, companies keep backup servers and switch to them automatically
Diversity: different servers run different operating systems to resist external attacks

lists.title: Problems with redundancy and diversity
items: Diversity and redundancy increase system complexity
Complexity raises the chance of error through unanticipated interactions and dependencies
Some engineers prefer simplicity and extensive verification and validation instead
Airbus flight control is redundant and diverse; the Boeing 777 has no software diversity

X04.answerKey: property, service requirement, costs and consequences
X04.commonError: Students read a percentage off the curve. It is on no page; the curve shows a trend, not a target.

X05.answerKey: a dated change record another engineer can reconstruct
X05.commonError: Students treat the five attributes as five names for documentation. Read each row as a different requirement on the process.
X05.answer: Choose the auditable row. Request a dated change record for the upgrade. It should link the reviewed requirements, test results, independent reviewer and release decision. The filename, version and owner must let another engineer reconstruct how this release was approved.
rows: People outside the process can understand it, check that standards are followed and suggest improvements.
The process includes redundant and diverse verification and validation activities.
A defined process model sets out the activities and the documents each activity produces.
The process can recover from failures of individual process activities.
A comprehensive set of development standards covers software production and documentation.

lists.title: Process diversity and redundancy
items: Validation should not depend on a single approach, such as testing
Redundant and diverse process activities matter most for verification and validation
Different activities that complement each other allow cross-checking and avoid process errors

R18.answerKey: test-first plus a linked release record
R18.commonError: Students answer “we would have tested more”. Ask which of three they mean: a named approver, an exercised rollback, or a staged release.

CHECK2.concept: what a second identical server protects against
CHECK2.commonError: Students say the second server doubles reliability. Ask which failures it shares with the first: the faulty requirements.
CHECK2.takeaway: A second identical server protects against independent hardware faults, not against the requirements both share.
CHECK2.question: Two identical servers share the same faulty requirements. What does the second server protect against?
CHECK2.sourceLabel: Course addition · not from the textbook · applies the chapter to the case

X06.commonError: Students ask for model checking here. Keep the four source activities; model checking comes two slides later.
X06.question: Which activity checks the specification before any code exists?
X06.answer: Specification analysis and proof. It checks properties of the specification before implementation. It cannot show that the requirements captured every real-world need.
X06.question2: Which activity checks a program against its specification?
X06.answer2: Program verification. It proves that the program conforms to its specification. Agreement with the specification does not show that every user need was captured.

lists.title: Formal methods include
items: Formal specification
Specification analysis and proof
Transformational development
Program verification

lists.title: Use of formal methods
items: Their principal benefit is fewer faults in systems
Their main area is dependable systems engineering, with several successful projects
They are most likely to pay off where failure costs are high

X06A.answerKey: verification-based; refinement transforms step by step
X06A.commonError: Students think a proof of agreement checks the requirements. Both routes still depend on the specification and its assumptions.

lists.title: Formal approaches
items: Verification-based: a specification and a program are proved equivalent, which shows the absence of implementation errors
Refinement-based: a representation is transformed step by step into a lower-level one, so a correct transformation keeps them equivalent

bullets: Prove that a specification and a program agree.
Transform the specification step by step into an implementation.
Both depend on the specification and the environment assumptions.

X06B.answerKey: a violating trace in the model
X06B.commonError: Students take a clean model-checking run as proof the plant is safe. Ask what the model assumes about the sensor and the operator.
X06B.question: For the switch-over model, what would a counterexample show?
X06B.answer: A reachable sequence that breaks the stated property. For example, both channels unavailable while the model requires supply. That would challenge the modelled switch-over logic. No model-checking run is claimed in this teaching example.
X06B.question2: Name one real-world assumption that the model cannot establish by itself.
X06B.answer2: Sensor accuracy. The model also cannot establish a complete model of the environment or actual operator behaviour. Each needs separate evidence.

lists.title: Classes of error found by formal methods
items: Specification and design errors: a formal model reveals requirement gaps, and model checking finds bad states such as deadlock
Inconsistencies between a specification and a program: refinement avoids them and program proving discovers them

lists.title: Acceptance of formal methods
items: Problem owners cannot read a formal specification, so they cannot judge whether it is accurate
The costs are easy to assess but the benefits are hard to assess, so managers hesitate
Engineers are unfamiliar with the approach and reluctant to propose it
Formal methods are still hard to scale up to large systems
Formal specification does not fit well with agile methods

APPLY.concept: decision with evidence, limit and owner
APPLY.answerKey: hold or revert pending the verified reading, with an owner
APPLY.commonError: Students fill every box with an opinion. Sample the reasoning: which fact is given, which evidence is requested, and who owns the decision.
bullets: State what can be justified now.
Name a real source or an observation from the case.
Identify what is unknown and what would change the decision.
APPLY.takeaway: A decision with limits needs evidence, a stated limit and an owner, not another opinion.
APPLY.answer: One defensible request is an independently verified pressure reading matched to the alarm and switch-over log. It helps separate a real pressure excursion from a sensor fault. Pending that evidence, state a hold or revert decision with its owner and the condition for resuming operation. This is one defensible approach, not the only acceptable decision. Separate facts from requested evidence and name the limit of the claim. Name who must be told: the next shift, the utility and, if drinking water could be affected, the public. The detector may help operators rank alarms. It must not by itself suppress protection. Count it as evidence only with an independent input and plant-specific evidence that its scores mean what they claim.
APPLY.title: Apply it · defend one decision with limits
APPLY.sourceLabel: Course addition · not from the textbook · applies the chapter to the case

CHALLENGE.answerKey: agreement from one transmitter is not independence
CHALLENGE.commonError: Students keep their first answer and add the detector as a third vote. Ask what all three readings share: one transmitter.
bullets: Both readings and the AI detector depend on one transmitter.
Three agreeing sources, one measurement: explain what changes.
Limit the claim, request an independently verified reading and name who accepts the revised scope.
CHALLENGE.answer: The two readings share one cause, so agreement cannot establish independence. A defensible revision withholds an unqualified approval. It requests an independently verified pressure reading matched to the logs. Name the observation that could change that decision and a human reviewer. When AI is used, its draft is not completed verification evidence. The detector's 0.91 adds no independent evidence either: it reads the same transmitter. Remove it from the evidence for this claim, or give it an independent input, and say so in the revision. Other decisions with limits can be defensible if their assumptions are explicit. Saying plainly what changed in your reasoning is part of the answer, not a weakness in it.
CHALLENGE.sourceLabel: Course addition · not from the textbook · applies the chapter to the case

stations.answerKey: the detector's label is a hypothesis, not evidence
stations.think: Devices down. Which evidence separates a real pressure excursion from a sensing fault, and does the AI label count?
stations.pair: Name one assumption and one given fact you need to support your answer.
stations.write: Write your claim and its evidence. Mark any test you only propose as proposed.
stations.hint: Name the service or property first. Use a source definition and the given facts. Ask which missing fact would change your claim. Decide whether the AI detector's label is an observation or an inference.
stations.note: Think without devices, then pair. Choosing when not to use technology is part of using it well. Use the same card; nobody is marked on field length or a timer.
stations.answer: An answer with limits separates the given facts from the needed evidence. A source explanation supports a mechanism. It does not prove the fictional plant passed a test. The detector's label is an inference, not an observation. Until you know its inputs and its validated performance on this plant, record it as a hypothesis, not as evidence.

criteria.name: Names the mechanism
levels: Names the chapter mechanism that decides the case and says how it applies.
Names a mechanism but does not connect it to the case facts.
No chapter mechanism, or the wrong one.

criteria.name: Uses only the given facts
levels: Every statement rests on a given fact or is marked as an assumption.
Mostly given facts, but one invented or unmarked assumption.
Relies on facts the case does not give.

criteria.name: Evidence another person can check
levels: Names evidence a second engineer could inspect, and marks proposed tests as proposed.
Names evidence, but it is vague or its status is unclear.
Opinion or confidence instead of evidence.

rubric.marks: 2 marks per criterion, 6 in total. Not graded in class. The same reasoning earns the assignment points.

strong.text: Claim: we cannot yet tell a real excursion from a sensor fault. Evidence: the alarm log and the switch-over log are given; an independently verified pressure reading is proposed. The AI label is a hypothesis until its inputs are known.
strong.why: Names the mechanism (failure cause), keeps to the given facts and proposes a checkable observation.

weak.text: It is a sensor fault because the AI said 0.91 and the software was just upgraded.
weak.why: Treats an inference as evidence; the upgrade is a hypothesis presented as a fact.

rubric.other: Other answers are accepted when they use a chapter mechanism and rest on the given facts. They must also name evidence someone else can check. A different decision with those three is as strong as the model answer.

stations.concept: diversity in input, not only algorithm
stations.answerKey: a second transmitter is diverse in sensing; the detector may not be
stations.think: Compare two mechanisms: a physically separate second transmitter, or the AI detector as a diverse check. Which one would you choose?
stations.pair: Ask your partner to argue for the mechanism you rejected. Name one trade-off and one thing both mechanisms share.
stations.write: Write why your mechanism supports your claim, and what you are still unsure of.
stations.hint: Explain why the mechanism affects your claim. Then name a shared cause, a mismatch or a limit outside its evidence.
stations.answer: Tie the chosen mechanism to the required property. Say what the alternative improves or sacrifices. Evidence of a shared dependency or mismatched assumption can defeat an apparently stronger design. The detector is diverse in algorithm but may not be diverse in input. A second, independently powered transmitter is diverse in sensing. It costs installation and validation.

criteria.name: Links the mechanism to the property
levels: Explains how the chosen mechanism affects the property at stake.
Names the mechanism without the link to the property.

criteria.name: Names a shared cause or limit
levels: Names a specific shared cause, mismatch or limit that could defeat the mechanism.
Mentions a limit in general terms only.
Treats the mechanism as always enough.

criteria.name: States the trade-off
levels: Says what the alternative improves and what it costs.
Gives one side of the trade-off only.

rubric.marks: 2 marks per criterion, 6 in total. Not graded in class. The same reasoning earns the assignment points.

strong.text: A second, independently powered transmitter, because reliability of the reading needs a different sensing path. Its limit: it still needs calibration and validation. The detector is cheaper but may read the same input.
strong.why: Links the mechanism to the property, names the shared-input limit and states the cost.

weak.text: Use the AI detector: it is a different algorithm, so it is diverse.
weak.why: Confuses algorithm diversity with input diversity; no limit and no trade-off.

rubric.other: Other answers are accepted when they use a chapter mechanism and rest on the given facts. They must also name evidence someone else can check. A different decision with those three is as strong as the model answer.

stations.answerKey: three readings of one transmitter count as one
stations.think: Two nominally separate readings use the same transmitter and power supply. The vendor's notes show the AI detector scores the signal from that same transmitter. Does your first decision still hold?
stations.pair: Explain what changes in your claim, your evidence or its scope.
stations.write: Record the new evidence and your revised decision with its limits. Say plainly what your first card got wrong. Name the responsible role and who must be told.
stations.hint: Do not simply repeat your first answer. Name the changed assumption, the next evidence and the condition that would change your decision.
stations.note: Classroom version only. The assessed assignment has its own new evidence, revealed after you commit.
stations.answer: The new fact changes the stated assumption, so the original evidence cannot be widened silently. Retain, restrict or revise the decision with a reason, a new verification requirement and a named owner. The AI detector's agreement is a third reading of the same transmitter. It cannot be counted as independent confirmation.

criteria.name: Says what the new fact changes
levels: Names the assumption the new fact breaks and what it leaves intact.
Notes the new fact without saying which assumption it breaks.
Ignores or restates the new fact.

criteria.name: Revises with a reason
levels: Keeps, changes or replaces the decision for a reason from the new fact. Says what the first answer got wrong.
Changes the decision without a clear reason, or hides the first answer.

criteria.name: Names the owner and who is told
levels: Names the role that decides and the people who must be informed.
Names neither the owner nor who is told.

rubric.marks: 2 marks per criterion, 6 in total. Not graded in class. The same reasoning earns the assignment points.

strong.text: My first card counted the two readings as independent; they share one transmitter and one power supply. Revise: hold the release and request a reading from a separate instrument. The plant manager decides; the next shift and the utility are told.
strong.why: Names the broken assumption, revises with a reason, admits the first error, names owner and audience.

weak.text: Keep my answer: three sources agree, so it is a sensor fault.
weak.why: Ignores the shared transmitter; names nobody.

rubric.other: Other answers are accepted when they use a chapter mechanism and rest on the given facts. They must also name evidence someone else can check. A different decision with those three is as strong as the model answer.

quiz.why: Availability and reliability are defined as probabilities that can be measured. Safety, security and resilience are judgments that must be argued from evidence.

hints.bound: An observable condition, something you would see, that ends the claim.

aiAssignment.scenario: A hospital adds an AI dose-check assistant to its medication cabinets. Before a nurse dispenses a drug, the assistant flags doses it predicts are unusual. The pharmacy's rule engine also checks each dose against the drug library. Management wants to report that dispensing is now “highly dependable”.
aiAssignment.stress: An audit finds that the AI assistant and the rule engine both read the same drug-library file. That file lists one high-risk drug in the wrong unit. Both checks agreed that a tenfold overdose was normal.

criteria.name: FIT
levels: Names the chapter concept that decides the case and shows why it fits these facts.
Names the right concept, with only a partial link to the facts.
Names a concept but does not connect it to the case.
No chapter concept, or the wrong one.

criteria.name: BOUND
levels: States an observable condition that would end the claim.
Names a condition, but nobody could easily observe it.
Gives a vague limit, such as “if it fails”.

criteria.name: ACT + EVIDENCE
levels: One concrete action with an owner, and evidence another engineer could inspect even if the AI is wrong.
A concrete action, but the evidence is weak or its status is unclear.
General advice, or evidence that relies on the AI's own output.

criteria.name: REFIT
levels: Uses the new information, names the assumption it broke and justifies retain, revise or replace.
Uses the new information but does not name the broken assumption.
Keeps or changes the answer without a reason.

criteria.name: OWNER + AI USE
levels: Names the role that accepts the risk and who must be told. Declares any AI help and how it was checked.
Names a role, but not who must be told, or the AI declaration is incomplete.
Names “the team” or “the system” as owner.
No owner and no AI declaration.

rubric.marks: Practice only · not graded · score yourself 1, 0.75, 0.5 or 0 per criterion

strong.text: Claim: dispensing is not shown to be highly dependable. Both checks read the same drug library, so they are not independent. The claim ends if a library error reaches a dispensed dose. Action: the pharmacy lead adds a second, separately maintained unit check. Evidence: a test log with a planted wrong-unit entry, proposed. After the audit I revise: the two checks share one cause.
strong.why: Names common cause and independence, gives an observable limit, an owner and checkable evidence, and revises with a reason.

weak.text: The system is dependable because no patient was harmed in three months and both checks passed the vendor tests.
weak.why: Treats absence of harm and vendor tests as proof; no limit, no owner, ignores the shared library.

rubric.other: they use a chapter concept, rest on the given facts and name evidence someone else can check. A different verdict that meets these conditions is as strong as the strong example.
